Richmond Fire Department
joining:
Open to Richmond residents. Meet a current firefighter first, then submit an application and start attending meetings and training while a background check and physical go through. A six-month probationary period ends with a vote of the current members.

Business meeting is the first Monday of the month, 7–9.30pm. Training is the third and fourth Mondays, same hours. Members respond to calls as they are available.

Pay starts at $15.01 an hour for training attended and calls answered, with first-responder discounts and benefits.

Source: the department's own joining page, richmondvt.gov, read September 2026.
burnPermits:
Vermont requires a Permit to Kindle Fire from the town's Forest Fire Warden for anything larger than a campfire. Two exceptions: when snow covers the ground at the burn site, and when the fire is at least 200 feet from anything that will carry flame. Wardens can suspend burning outright when fire danger is high.

In Richmond, permits go through Shelburne Dispatch: 802-985-8051.

The warden system dates to 1904, when Vermont made each town responsible for preventing and fighting its own forest fires under a warden appointed by the Commissioner of Forests, Parks and Recreation with the selectboard's approval. Wardens serve five-year terms.

Sources: richmondvt.gov; Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation.
history:
Dennis Gile retired in 2025 after nine years as chief and fifty-seven years with the department. Jerry Levesque was appointed to succeed him and has put the department's attention on recruiting and keeping firefighters. A study of the department was carried out in early 2025; the chief and the selectboard are working from it.

The department is wholly owned by the Town of Richmond — the town owns the building and the equipment, and the members are volunteers paid an hourly rate for calls and training.

Source: Town of Richmond, 231st Annual Report, fiscal year 2024–2025.
callsNote:
Not obtained. Vermont requires every department to report its incidents to the state under 20 V.S.A., but the Division of Fire Safety publishes statewide totals only — 26,778 EMS calls across Vermont in 2024, against 28,057 in 2023 — with no breakdown by department. The VFIRS system that holds the per-department figures is open to fire departments, not to the public.

Richmond's own numbers would come from a public records request to the Division of Fire Safety, or from asking the department.
budgetNote:
Richmond voters approved $446,154 for the fire department in fiscal year 2026 — 3.37% less than the $461,718 budgeted the year before, out of a total town budget of $4,870,565.

Two fifths of it never reaches an incident. $180,000 goes to the capital reserve and $58,572 pays down the 2018 engine, principal and interest, which is what a town of four thousand people does instead of buying a fire truck outright. Salaries — the hourly rate members are paid for calls and training — come to $70,000, up 22.81% on the year. The single new line is $25,000 for a needs assessment of the department, the study the chief and selectboard have been working from.

A separate $38,033 sits under town administration as "fire protection". That is the fee the town pays its own water and wastewater department for fire flow, not money the fire department spends.

Source: Town of Richmond, FY26 Budgeted Expenses, presented to the selectboard January 2025.
